governments.later_changes: Ben-Gurion resigned 15 Oct 1950 over disputes with the United Religious Front on education policy in immigrant camps.
Reshuffle of the first government after a Knesset dispute over registration of schoolchildren; same coalition parties retained.
Agudat Yisrael and Poalei Agudat Yisrael left the coalition on 23 Sept 1952 over conscription, reducing it to 60/120 seats; government resigned 19 Dec 1952 over religious education dispute.
Ben-Gurion dropped Agudat Yisrael and Poalei Agudat Yisrael, replacing them with the General Zionists and Progressive Party.
Sharett succeeded Ben-Gurion as PM with the same coalition; fell 29 Jun 1955 when the General Zionists refused to back the government in a no-confidence vote.
Sharett dropped the General Zionists and Progressive Party from the coalition (one Progressive minister stayed on individually).
Ben-Gurion resigned 31 Dec 1957 after demanding Ahdut HaAvoda ministers resign over an information leak; government stayed in place about a week until the 8th government formed.
NRP ministers left 1 Jul 1958; Ahdut HaAvoda and Mapam left 5 Jul 1959 over an arms deal with West Germany, precipitating Ben-Gurion's resignation.
Largely a continuation of the 8th government's coalition, adding the Arab satellite lists Progress and Development and Cooperation and Brotherhood; fell 31 Jan 1961 on a no-confidence motion.
Ben-Gurion resigned 16 Jun 1963 citing personal reasons; this was his final term as PM.
Eshkol continued Ben-Gurion's coalition unchanged as a 'government of continuity'; resigned 14 Dec 1964 amid the Lavon Affair dispute.
Same coalition retained; Yosef Almogi and Shimon Peres resigned in May 1965 over the Mapai-Ahdut HaAvoda alliance.
Gahal and Rafi joined on the eve of the Six-Day War (5 Jun 1967), turning it into a broad national-unity government; Eshkol died in office 26 Feb 1969.
Formed after Eshkol's death, retaining the national-unity coalition inherited from the 13th government.
First government to serve a full four-year term; Gahal left in Aug 1970 over acceptance of the Rogers Plan, ending the unity arrangement.
Shortest-lived Israeli government (85 days); Meir resigned 11 Apr 1974 after the Agranat Commission's interim Yom Kippur War report, remaining caretaker until Rabin formed the 17th government.
National Religious Party joined 30 Oct 1974 (+10 seats); Ratz left 6 Nov 1974; NRP resigned 22 Dec 1976 leaving the government in caretaker status until the 1977 election.

Corrected: at the 20 Jun 1977 confidence vote the coalition already effectively included Shlomtzion (2 seats, Ariel Sharon became Minister of Agriculture), giving 61/120, a bare majority; Shlomtzion's formal merger into Likud followed on 5 Jul 1977. Moshe Dayan (elected on the Alignment list) joined as Foreign Minister as an independent MK, and Shmuel Flatto-Sharon (1 seat) gave informal support in connection with his parliamentary-immunity request; neither is confirmed as a formal coalition seat and both are left out of seats_total (see gaps). Dash joined the coalition in Oct 1977 with 15 seats, giving a working majority of about 76/120, before deteriorating internally and largely leaving by Sep 1978.
Coalition held 63 of 120 seats at formation; Tehiya joined 26 Aug 1981, raising ministerial posts from 17 to 18.

governments.later_changes: Coalition held 62 of 120 seats after Begin's resignation; Mordechai Ben-Porat (Renewal of Social Zionism) departed 31 Jan 1984.
Grand national-unity coalition (97/120 seats) with a Peres-Shamir PM rotation agreement; Shamir took over as PM on schedule 20 Oct 1986.
Continuation of the unity government under the rotation deal, with Shamir replacing Peres as PM; Shinui departed 26 May 1987.
Alignment left 15 Mar 1990 after Shamir rejected the Baker peace initiative and a no-confidence motion (60-55) toppled the government, the only time this has happened in Israeli history.
Narrow right-religious coalition of 62/120 seats; Tzomet left 31 Dec 1991, Moledet and Tehiya left 21 Jan 1992, all in protest of Shamir's participation in the Madrid Conference.
Shas left the coalition 14 Sep 1993 (remaining as outside support for some period); Rabin assassinated 4 Nov 1995, Peres took over as interim PM under the same government.
Formed after Rabin's assassination with Peres continuing as PM; coalition (58/120 seats) relied on 5 outside-support seats from Hadash and the Arab Democratic Party.
Gesher left the Likud-Gesher-Tzomet bloc's coalition role on 6 Jan 1998. Labor was the single largest Knesset party (34 seats) but sat in opposition.

United Torah Judaism left in Sep 1999 over Shabbat transport of a power-station turbine; the government deteriorated further after the Second Intifada broke out, leading to a special PM election in Feb 2001.

Formed after a special PM-only election (no parallel Knesset vote), so Knesset seat shares carried over from 1999; Shas left 23 May 2002, returned 3 Jun 2002; Labor-Meimad exited 2 Nov 2002, ending the government.

Formed with 60/120 seats, one short of a majority; National Religious Party joined 3 Mar 2003 (+6, reaching 66). National Union left Jun 2004, NRP left Nov 2004, Shinui left Dec 2004; Labor-Meimad joined Jan 2005 and left Nov 2005; Likud itself formally left in Jan 2006 as Sharon founded Kadima.
Yisrael Beiteinu joined Nov 2006 (11 seats) and left 16 Jan 2008 over Palestinian peace talks; Labor's Raleb Majadele became the first Muslim minister, 29 Jan 2007.

United Torah Judaism joined 1 Apr 2009 (+5, reaching 74 total). Labor left 17 Jan 2011 (Barak's 'Independence' breakaway kept supporting the government); Kadima joined 8 May 2012 and left 17 Jul 2012 over the Tal Law. Kadima was the single largest Knesset party (28 seats) but sat in opposition at formation.
Coalition collapsed 2 Dec 2014 when Netanyahu dismissed Yair Lapid (Finance) and Tzipi Livni (Justice); remaining Yesh Atid ministers resigned soon after, triggering new elections.

Yisrael Beiteinu and the New Right (after splitting from Jewish Home) joined 29 Dec 2018. This government continued in caretaker form through two elections (Apr 2019, Sep 2019) that produced no new government before finally being replaced in May 2020.

Corrected: Blue and White (Kahol Lavan) split on 26 Mar 2020 when Yesh Atid (13 seats) and Telem (5 seats, minus 2 MKs who broke off as Derekh Eretz) left; only Gantz's Israel Resilience faction (15 seats), still using the 'Blue and White' Knesset-faction name, joined this government. Only 2 of Labor's 3 MKs (Peretz, Shmuli) joined; Merav Michaeli stayed in opposition. The Jewish Home (1 seat, formerly part of the Yamina list) joined separately from the rest of Yamina. Emergency unity/rotation government formed under COVID-19 pressure; part of the Labor Party joined Jan 2021 (2 of its 3 MKs) and left again before the government's Jun 2021 collapse.

Ideologically diverse 'change government' with a Bennett-Lapid PM rotation; Lapid became PM 1 Jul 2022. Collapsed Jun-Jun 2022 over West Bank settler-law legislation; no member parties changed before dissolution.

Coalition members have shifted repeatedly since formation: Noam joined 29 Dec 2022, left 28 Feb 2023, rejoined 25 May 2023, left 24 Mar 2025; National Unity joined 12 Oct 2023, left 9 Jun 2024; New Hope left 25 Mar 2024, rejoined 29 Sep 2024; Otzma Yehudit left 21 Jan 2025, rejoined 19 Mar 2025; United Torah Judaism left 15 Jul 2025; Shas left government (retaining coalition/Knesset support) 17 Jul 2025. As of Sep 2026 this remains the government of record pending the Oct 2026 election.

no_government_elections.outcome: Netanyahu secured the mandate with 65 recommendations but failed to form a coalition over Haredi conscription-exemption disputes; Knesset voted 74-45 to dissolve itself (29 May 2019); new election called for 17 Sep 2019.

Netanyahu got the first mandate (25 Sep 2019) and returned it unused 22 Oct; Gantz then failed after 28 days (returned 21 Nov); no MK formed a government by the 11 Dec deadline, so the Knesset dissolved itself again; new election called for 2 Mar 2020.

Mandate log: dates for the 2013, 2015 and 2022 mandate-granting events are drawn from a mix of the relevant government's Wikipedia page and secondary press coverage (Forward, Al Jazeera, CQ Press), since the government pages themselves often omit the mandate date; treat these as reasonably well-sourced but secondary to the primary per-government Wikipedia pages used elsewhere in this file.
